title: 'Saffron-robed' Dawn
greek: Ἠὼς μὲν κροκόπεπλος ἐκίδνατο πᾶσαν ἐπ᾽ αἶαν (Ēōs men krokopeplos ekidnato pasan ep' aian)
short: Dawn's epithet krokopeplos, 'with saffron (yellow) robe', pictures the yellow light of morning spreading over all the earth.
body: krokopeplos combines krokos, the saffron crocus, and peplos, a woman's robe; LSJ renders it 'with yellow veil'. It describes Dawn here and at the openings of Books 19, 23 (227) and 24 (695), and complements the more familiar 'rosy-fingered' (rhododaktylos), used of Dawn earlier in the poem. Where 'rosy-fingered' catches the first streaks of light, 'saffron-robed' catches the full yellow spread of morning across the sky, the robe 'spread over the face of all the earth'. Hesiod applies the epithet to other goddesses, Enyo and a river nymph (Theogony 273, 358). Zenodotus omitted this line here and placed it after 8.52 (Leaf), which would make Zeus' assembly take place the night before.

title: Zeus forbids the gods to fight; 'the Cut-short Battle'
greek: Ζεὺς δὲ θεῶν ἀγορὴν ποιήσατο τερπικέραυνος (Zeus de theōn agorēn poiēsato terpikeraunos)
short: Zeus bans every god from the war, beginning the Trojan success he promised Thetis; ancient readers called Book 8 'the Cut-short Battle'.
body: The scholia called this book kolos machē, 'the curtailed battle', because the narrative is compressed and breaks off abruptly at nightfall (Schol. B, quoted by Leaf). Book 8 finally puts into effect the promise Zeus nodded to Thetis (1.524-30): the Greeks must suffer until Achilles is honoured. Leaf saw the book as a bridge composed to introduce the Embassy of Book 9, noting that nearly a third of its lines recur elsewhere in Homer, though he grants it 'great spirit and movement'. Zeus' speech is pure assertion of power, with threats of Tartarus and the challenge of the golden cord. Aristarchus athetized Athena's conciliatory reply and Zeus' indulgent smile (8.28-40), because the lines are assembled from other passages and undercut the force of his threats, which he later shows he meant (8.397ff).

title: Tartarus
greek: Τάρταρον ἠερόεντα (Tartaron ēeroenta)
short: The deepest pit beneath the earth, with iron gates and a bronze threshold, as far below Hades as heaven is above earth: Zeus' prison for rebel gods.
body: Zeus threatens to hurl any disobedient god into 'murky' Tartarus, a gulf far below Hades. Leaf notes the unmistakable echoes in Hesiod's Theogony: Tartarus lies 'as far beneath the earth as heaven is above earth' (Theog. 720), is ringed by a bronze fence, has bronze gates set by Poseidon, and 'marble gates and a bronze threshold' (811). He also compares the same threat in the Homeric Hymn to Hermes (256-9) and cannot tell which passage borrowed from which. The Titans are imprisoned there, among them Iapetus and Cronos, whom Zeus mentions later in this book (8.478-81; cf. 14.279). The speech maps a vertical cosmos of heaven, earth, Hades and Tartarus, a scheme Milton adapts when he places his hell 'as far removed from God and light of Heav'n / As from the Center thrice to th' utmost Pole' (Paradise Lost 1.73-4).

title: The golden chain (cord) of Zeus
greek: σειρὴν χρυσείην ἐξ οὐρανόθεν κρεμάσαντες (seirēn chryseiēn ex ouranothen kremasantes)
short: Zeus dares the gods to pull on a golden cord hung from heaven; he could haul them up with earth and sea. Philosophers later made it the chain of being.
body: The challenge is a cosmic tug-of-war proving that Zeus outweighs all other powers combined. seirē means a cord or rope (LSJ). Leaf sees in it only a trial of strength 'by pulling at a rope', and the gold simply as a mark of divinity, yet the line was allegorised from early times. In Plato's Theaetetus (153c-d) Socrates says that by the golden cord Homer means nothing but the sun; the Neoplatonists took it up, and medieval alchemists spoke of the 'aurea catena Homeri' as the chain of all existences (Leaf). Milton remembers it when the newly created world hangs 'in a golden Chain' from heaven (Paradise Lost 2.1051-2). Zenodotus athetized 8.25-6 on the ground that a peak of Olympus cannot hold up the earth of which it is part; Leaf takes this as a sign that the poet imagines Olympus as heaven rather than a mountain in Thessaly.

title: Ida and Gargarus
greek: Ἴδην δ᾽ ἵκανεν πολυπίδακα, μητέρα θηρῶν, Γάργαρον· ἔνθα δέ οἱ τέμενος βωμός τε θυήεις (Idēn d' hikanen polypidaka, mētera thērōn, Gargaron; entha de hoi temenos bōmos te thyēeis)
short: Zeus drives to Mount Ida, 'many-fountained, mother of wild beasts', and its peak Gargarus, where he has a sacred precinct and altar, to watch the battle.
body: Ida is the mountain range south-east of Troy, the source of its rivers. Gargarus is one of its peaks; Leaf notes the others were Lectum (14.284) and, according to Callimachus, Phalacra. The phrase 'to Ida... to Gargarus' is a whole-and-part figure, like 'to Cyprus... to Paphos' in the Odyssey (8.362-3). The demesne is a temenos, land 'cut off' (temnō) and assigned to a king or god (LSJ); with the 'fragrant altar' it implies a cult of Zeus on Ida, and Greeks at prayer address him as 'Father Zeus, that rulest from Ida' (3.276, 7.202). From this vantage point Zeus watches city and ships, thunders through the battle (8.75, 8.170), and is later seduced there by Hera (14.292-353). His golden-maned horses, golden armour and whip stress divine splendour.

title: The golden scales of Zeus
greek: χρύσεια πατὴρ ἐτίταινε τάλαντα, ἐν δ᾽ ἐτίθει δύο κῆρε τανηλεγέος θανάτοιο (chryseia patēr etitaine talanta, en d' etithei dyo kēre tanēlegeos thanatoio)
short: At noon Zeus weighs two 'fates of death' for Trojans and Achaeans; the Achaean doom sinks, signalling their defeat.
body: Zeus holds out the golden balance, puts a kēr, a doom or death-spirit, for each army in the pans, and lifts it by the middle; the Achaeans' 'day of doom' sinks to earth. The same lines return at 22.209-13, when Hector's doom sinks and Apollo abandons him. Leaf argues that the weighing is less a consultation of some power above Zeus than his declaration that the turning-point has come: the result is never in doubt, and the question whether fate or Zeus is supreme would have meant little to Homer's audience. The scene had a long afterlife. The scholia report that Aeschylus wrote a Psychostasia in which Zeus weighed the souls of Memnon and Achilles; Virgil's Jupiter weighs Turnus and Aeneas (Aen. 12.725-7); and Milton's God hangs out 'his golden Scales' (Paradise Lost 4.996-1004). Aristarchus athetized 8.73-4, which Leaf also finds indefensible: their dual verb implies two fates for each side.

title: Nestor, 'warder of the Achaeans'
greek: Νέστωρ οἶος ἔμιμνε Γερήνιος, οὖρος Ἀχαιῶν (Nestōr oios emimne Gerēnios, ouros Achaiōn)
short: Nestor, 'guardian of the Achaeans', is the only Greek who stays when panic strikes, and only because Paris has shot one of his horses.
body: ouros here is not the common word for 'fair wind' but a separate noun meaning 'watcher, warder, guardian', related to horaō, 'see' (Middle Liddell). The narrator immediately undercuts the grand title: Nestor stays 'nowise of his own will', because Paris' arrow has struck his trace-horse in the brain. Leaf explains that the old man is cutting the traces (parēoriai) of this extra trace-horse, which Homer mentions only here and at 16.152, while Hector's chariot bears down on him. The moment sets up a rescue that defines the young Diomedes: he alone stands firm, calls on Odysseus in vain, and takes Nestor into his own chariot, offering to show him the swift Trojan horses he captured from Aeneas in Book 5 (Leaf on 8.105-8).

title: Did Odysseus hear Diomedes?
greek: οὐδ᾽ ἐσάκουσε πολύτλας δῖος Ὀδυσσεύς (oud' esakouse polytlas dios Odysseus)
short: Did Odysseus fail to hear Diomedes' call, or refuse to heed it? Ancient critics debated whether Homer shows him as a coward here.
body: Diomedes shouts at Odysseus for fleeing 'like a coward in the throng'. The verb esakouō occurs only here in Homer. Aristarchus took it as 'did not hearken', so Odysseus deliberately ignored the call; others argued that Homer never makes a leading Greek hero a downright coward, so it must mean 'did not hear'. Leaf adds a parallel from Thucydides (4.34), where the word is used of soldiers unable to catch orders in the din of battle, which favours 'did not hear', but he remarks that the panic sent by Zeus would hardly excuse Odysseus when Diomedes manages to resist it. Leaf also suggests that 'turning thy back' (meta nōta balōn) may mean slinging the shield onto the back for retreat. The episode fits Odysseus' reputation for prudence rather than rash courage, in contrast with his lone stand at 11.401-10.

title: Zeus' thunderbolts in Book 8
greek: βροντήσας δ᾽ ἄρα δεινὸν ἀφῆκ᾽ ἀργῆτα κεραυνόν (brontēsas d' ara deinon aphēk' argēta keraunon)
short: Zeus turns the battle again and again with thunder and lightning: Book 8 is driven by direct divine force rather than by heroes' victories.
body: Leaf observes that 'a free use of thunder and lightning is characteristic of this book'. At noon Zeus thunders from Ida and sends a blazing flash among the Achaeans (8.75-7). Here, when Diomedes threatens to rout the Trojans, he hurls a bolt in front of Diomedes' horses, raising a flame of 'burning sulphur'; the smell of sulphur after lightning appears also at 14.415 (Leaf). When Diomedes thinks of turning to fight, Zeus thunders three times as 'a sign' (8.169-71). Nestor reads the omen correctly: 'a man may in no wise thwart the purpose of Zeus' (8.143-4). Leaf notes that the rapid reversals of fortune in this book are produced not, as in other battles, by the victories of heroes, but by repeated interference from Zeus. The thunderbolt (keraunos) is Zeus' distinctive weapon, made for him by the Cyclopes in Hesiod (Theog. 139-41, 501-6).

title: Seat, meat and cup: the marks of honour
greek: ἕδρῃ τε κρέασίν τε ἰδὲ πλείοις δεπάεσσι (hedrēi te kreasin te ide pleiois depaessi)
short: Hector taunts Diomedes that the Greeks will no longer honour him with the chief seat, the best meat and a cup always full.
body: These privileges, a front seat at the feast, choice portions of meat and a cup kept full, are the visible, material form of timē, honour. Sarpedon lists them at 12.310-21 and draws the moral that such honours oblige a prince to fight in the front rank; Agamemnon reminds Idomeneus that his cup always stands full (4.262-3). Leaf cross-refers these passages and Ajax's chine at 7.321. Hector's taunt turns on gender and status: 'thou art, it appeareth, no better than a woman', and if Diomedes flees he forfeits the honours that define him. Leaf remarks drily that Hector 'loses no time in justifying the opinion' of Nestor and Diomedes, who had just predicted his boasting (8.148-56).

title: glēnē: 'puppet', 'doll'
greek: ἔρρε, κακὴ γλήνη (erre, kakē glēnē)
short: Hector's insult glēnē literally means 'eyeball' or 'pupil'; here it seems to mean 'doll' or 'plaything', perhaps from the tiny figure seen reflected in an eye.
body: Elsewhere glēnē means the eyeball or pupil (14.494; Od. 9.390). Here it is a term of abuse: 'Off with you, wretched doll!' LSJ suggests 'doll, plaything', since figures are reflected small in the pupil, comparing korē, 'girl' and 'pupil' (Latin pupilla, 'little doll', developed the same way). Leaf instead derives the word from a root meaning 'bright', comparing glēnea, 'trinkets' (24.192), and reads 'you pretty toy'. Either way the insult reduces Diomedes to a decorative, unmanly object, continuing 'no better than a woman'. Aristarchus and Aristophanes athetized 8.164-6 as feeble and unsuited to the speakers, objecting also to the odd phrase 'I will give thee thy daimōn' (8.166, 'deal thee thy doom'); Leaf reports Bergk's reply that without these lines Hector's speech is jejune.

title: Hector's horses
greek: Ξάνθε τε καὶ σύ, Πόδαργε, καὶ Αἴθων Λάμπε τε δῖε (Xanthe te kai sy, Podarge, kai Aithōn Lampe te die)
short: Hector addresses four horses, 'Bay', 'Swift-foot', 'Blaze' and 'Shining', though Homeric chariots have a pair; Aristarchus rejected the line.
body: The names describe colour or speed: Xanthos 'yellow, bay', Podargos 'swift-foot' or 'white-foot', Aithōn 'blazing, tawny', Lampos 'bright'. Leaf notes that all of them occur elsewhere: Achilles' horse Xanthus and the mare Podarge (16.149-50), Menelaus' Podargus (23.295), and Lampus, one of the horses of Dawn (Od. 23.246). Aristarchus athetized 8.185 because Homer knows no four-horse chariots and the following verb is dual; Leaf keeps the line, suggesting the composer treated dual and plural as interchangeable. Hector reminds the horses that Andromache fed them honey-sweet wheat, and wine mixed for drinking, even before her husband. Aristophanes and Aristarchus rejected the wine line (8.189) as absurd; Leaf replies that without it Hector would seem to be eating the grain himself. The touch keeps the domestic Andromache of Book 6 in view.

title: Nestor's golden shield and Diomedes' breastplate
greek: ἀσπίδα Νεστορέην, τῆς νῦν κλέος οὐρανὸν ἵκει (aspida Nestoreēn, tēs nyn kleos ouranon hikei)
short: Hector longs to capture Nestor's all-gold shield, whose fame 'reaches to heaven', and Diomedes' breastplate made by Hephaestus: two treasures unknown elsewhere in the poem.
body: Leaf observes that a famous golden shield of Nestor 'is as little known elsewhere to the Iliad' as a divine breastplate of Diomedes. Diomedes had recently exchanged his bronze armour for Glaucus' gold (6.230-6), which makes a Hephaestus-made corslet harder still to place, and nothing is said of a gold shield among the arms Nestor won from Ereuthalion (7.146-55). Leaf explains the shield's kanones, 'rods', as its cross-bars or handles. Hector's hope that seizing these pieces would make the Greeks take to their ships that very night also conflicts with his aim elsewhere of burning the ships to stop their escape (8.182, 8.217). Leaf therefore treats 8.184-212 as a later expansion, though one substantially original rather than patched together from other passages.

title: Helice and Aegae, cult centres of Poseidon
greek: οἱ δέ τοι εἰς Ἑλίκην τε καὶ Αἰγὰς δῶρ᾽ ἀνάγουσι (hoi de toi eis Helikēn te kai Aigas dōr' anagousi)
short: Two towns on the coast of Achaea in the northern Peloponnese, chief seats of Poseidon's worship; Helice was later swallowed by the sea.
body: Hera rebukes Poseidon: the Danaans bring him many gracious offerings at Helice and Aegae, yet he will not help them. Leaf identifies both as cities of Achaea and chief seats of Poseidon's cult (cf. 2.575, 13.21, 20.404). At 13.21-2 Poseidon's golden palace lies in the depths at Aegae, and at 20.403-5 a dying man bellows like a bull dragged round the altar of 'the lord of Helice'. Helice itself was destroyed in 373 BC by an earthquake and a great wave; Strabo (8.7.2) and Pausanias (7.24) describe the disaster, which was blamed on Poseidon's anger, and Pausanias says the ruins could still be seen under water. Poseidon refuses to defy Zeus, who 'verily is mightier far'. Hera's epithet aptoepēs, 'reckless in speech', is of uncertain formation (LSJ).

title: The layout of the Greek camp
greek: στῆ δ᾽ ἐπ᾽ Ὀδυσσῆος μεγακήτεϊ νηῒ μελαίνῃ (stē d' ep' Odyssēos megakētei nēi melainēi)
short: Agamemnon shouts from Odysseus' ship in the middle of the line; Ajax and Achilles, the bravest, had beached their ships at the two exposed ends.
body: The beached fleet formed a long line along the shore. The ships of Ajax and Achilles were drawn up at the extreme ends, 'trusting in their valour and the strength of their hands', the most exposed positions. Odysseus' ship stood at the centre, so that a shout from it carried to both ends; in Book 11 it is also the place of assembly, justice and the altars (11.806-8), and Leaf notes the contradiction with 7.383, where the assembly gathers by Agamemnon's ship. Lines 8.222-6 recur at 11.5-9, and many manuscripts omit 224-6 here (Leaf). Agamemnon carries his great purple cloak in his hand; Leaf wonders whether this frees his movement or serves as a signal, and notes that purple is not yet a specifically royal colour in Homer. megakētēs is best taken as 'with mighty hollow' (Leaf).

title: Agamemnon's rebuke: the boasts on Lemnos
greek: αἰδώς, Ἀργεῖοι, κάκ᾽ ἐλέγχεα, εἶδος ἀγητοί ... ἃς ὁπότ᾽ ἐν Λήμνῳ κενεαυχέες ἠγοράασθε (aidōs, Argeioi, kak' elenchea, eidos agētoi ... has hopot' en Lēmnōi keneauchees ēgoraasthe)
short: Agamemnon shames the Greeks with their empty boasts over wine on Lemnos, then blames Zeus for blinding him with atē and prays for the army's survival.
body: He opens with the rallying cry 'Shame, Argives, base things of reproach, fair in semblance only' (elencheēs, 'cowardly, worthy of reproof', LSJ). On Lemnos, eating beef and drinking full bowls, each man had boasted he would face a hundred or two hundred Trojans. Leaf sees an allusion to the famous Lemnian wine (7.467); von Christ thought the episode came from the lost Cypria, which Leaf doubts. Aristarchus athetized 8.231 on the ground that beef does not make men boastful. Agamemnon then asks whether Zeus ever blinded a king with such atē, 'ruinous delusion'; Leaf calls blaming Zeus' atē 'a favourite resource of Agamemnon' (compare 2.111 and 19.86-94). He reminds Zeus of the fat and thigh-bones he burned on every altar on his way, and begs that at least the army may escape.

anchor: surest of omens among winged birds
title: The eagle and the fawn
greek: αὐτίκα δ᾽ αἰετὸν ἧκε, τελειότατον πετεηνῶν, νεβρὸν ἔχοντ᾽ ὀνύχεσσι (autika d' aieton hēke, teleiotaton peteēnōn, nebron echont' onychessi)
short: Zeus answers Agamemnon's tearful prayer with an eagle that drops a fawn beside his altar; the Greeks take heart and attack.
body: The eagle is Zeus' own bird, here called teleiotatos, 'most perfect' of birds; Leaf, following the scholia, takes this in the sense 'most sure of fulfilment' rather than physically perfect, and compares Aeschylus' address to 'Zeus Teleios', 'Zeus who fulfils' (Agamemnon 973). The eagle carries a fawn, the young of a swift hind, and drops it beside the altar where the Achaeans sacrificed to Zeus 'from whom all omens come'. The sign tells the army that Zeus has granted the minimum Agamemnon asked: the host will be saved and not perish (8.245-6). Bird omens are a principal form of Homeric divination; compare the eagle and snake of 12.200-50, an omen Hector famously dismisses with 'one omen is best, to fight for one's country'.

anchor: Zeus from whom all omens come
title: Zeus Panomphaios
greek: πανομφαίῳ Ζηνί (panomphaiōi Zēni)
short: Panomphaios, 'of all oracular voices', is a cult title of Zeus that occurs only here in Homer.
body: The word joins pan, 'all', and omphē, a divine voice or oracle. LSJ glosses it 'sender of ominous voices, author of divination'; Leaf explains it as the god to whom belong all omens given by sounds or voices, such as the ominous word Odysseus asks Zeus for at Od. 20.98-101, and adds that the title is 'certainly not very appropriate' to the bird omen just described. It was a real cult name: Ovid places an ancient altar 'sacred to the Panomphaean Thunderer' between Sigeum and Rhoeteum on the Trojan coast, near where Apollo and Poseidon built Laomedon's walls (Metamorphoses 11.197-8), and Simonides also uses the epithet (LSJ). Murray's 'from whom all omens come' is a paraphrase. The detail that the Greeks regularly sacrificed at this altar shows the camp equipped with its own sanctuaries.

anchor: as a child beneath his mother
title: Teucer under Ajax's shield
greek: αὐτὰρ ὁ αὖτις ἰών, πάϊς ὣς ὑπὸ μητέρα, δύσκεν εἰς Αἴανθ᾽ (autar ho autis iōn, pais hōs hypo mētera, dysken eis Aianth')
short: The archer Teucer shoots from behind his half-brother Ajax's great shield and runs back to it 'as a child to its mother': a tender simile in a killing scene.
body: Ajax moves his shield aside, Teucer spots a target and shoots, then ducks back under cover. Leaf calls the tactic characteristically oriental: Assyrian reliefs often show an archer crouching beside a warrior with a large shield, and Greek has the verb hypaspizein, 'to serve as shield-bearer', for the role. The simile reverses gender and scale, turning the giant Ajax into a mother and his tower-shield into a refuge. Teucer's 'back-bent bow' (palintona toxa) may be the double-curved 'Scythian' bow, or simply an elastic one (Leaf). His aristeia (8.266-334) is, Leaf thought, the most original episode of the book and probably older than the rest of it; it ends when Hector's jagged stone breaks his bowstring and numbs his wrist (8.324-9).

anchor: for all thou wast a bastard
title: Teucer, son of Telamon and Hesione
greek: καί σε νόθον περ ἐόντα κομίσσατο ᾧ ἐνὶ οἴκῳ (kai se nothon per eonta komissato hōi eni oikōi)
short: Agamemnon reminds Teucer that he is Telamon's illegitimate son, born, in later tradition, of the Trojan princess Hesione; ancient critics found the reminder tactless.
body: In the common tradition Heracles sacked Laomedon's Troy and gave Laomedon's daughter Hesione to Telamon as a prize, and she bore him Teucer (Apollodorus 2.6.4, 3.12.7). Teucer would thus be Priam's nephew, fighting against his mother's city; the name itself recalls the 'Teucrians', a name for the Trojans (Leaf). Zenodotus omitted 8.284, and Aristophanes and Aristarchus athetized it, as out of place and more likely to displease than encourage. Aristarchus thought Homer did not know the Hesione story, because Teucer is elsewhere called Ajax's kasignētos, a word commonly used of brothers by the same mother; Leaf answers that Polydorus is Hector's kasignētos although born of a different mother (20.419; 21.88-91). Agamemnon's point is generous all the same: Telamon reared the boy in his own house, and Teucer can repay him with glory.

title: The prize of honour (presbēion)
greek: πρώτῳ τοι μετ᾽ ἐμὲ πρεσβήϊον ἐν χερὶ θήσω (prōtōi toi met' eme presbēion en cheri thēsō)
short: Agamemnon promises Teucer the first prize after his own when Troy falls: a tripod, a chariot and horses, or a woman to share his bed.
body: presbēion, a 'prize for the first' after the king, occurs only here in Homer (Leaf; LSJ under presbeion); Leaf compares later formations such as prōteion and deutereion, 'first' and 'second prize'. Spoils were distributed by the commander, who took his own choice first, and his right to do so is the root of the quarrel with Achilles in Book 1. The list of possible prizes, a tripod, two horses with their chariot, or 'a woman that shall go up into thy bed', shows that captive women counted among movable goods, like Briseis and Chryseis. Teucer's reply, 'why urgest thou me on, that of myself am eager?', is a common Homeric response to encouragement, and he lists the eight men his arrows have hit (8.297-9).

title: Hector the 'mad dog'
greek: τοῦτον δ᾽ οὐ δύναμαι βαλέειν κύνα λυσσητῆρα (touton d' ou dynamai baleein kyna lyssētēra)
short: Teucer calls Hector a 'raging dog': lyssa, the madness of a rabid dog, is the Iliad's word for frenzied battle-fury.
body: lyssētēr, 'one that is raging or raving mad' (LSJ), comes from lyssa, which in Homer always means martial rage (LSJ): a 'mighty lyssa has entered' Hector (9.239), and lyssa grips Achilles' heart as he slaughters Trojans (21.542). Leaf notes that Hector is several times compared to a mad dog (cf. 9.239, 9.305, 13.53). Dog-words are among the sharpest insults in Homer: Achilles calls Agamemnon 'dog-eyed' (1.225), and Zeus calls Hera more 'doglike' than any other (8.483). The image of the rabid dog suits Hector's fury in this book, where his eyes become 'as the eyes of the Gorgon or of Ares' (8.349). Teucer's arrows miss Hector twice, the second time because Apollo turns them aside.

title: Simile: Gorgythion and the poppy
greek: μήκων δ᾽ ὡς ἑτέρωσε κάρη βάλεν, ἥ τ᾽ ἐνὶ κήπῳ, καρπῷ βριθομένη νοτίῃσί τε εἰαρινῇσιν (mēkōn d' hōs heterōse karē balen, hē t' eni kēpōi, karpōi brithomenē notiēisi te eiarinēisin)
short: Priam's son Gorgythion drops his helmeted head like a garden poppy weighed down with seed and spring rain: one of the Iliad's most famous death-similes.
body: Teucer, aiming at Hector, hits Gorgythion, son of Priam and Castianeira, a bride from Aesyme 'in form like to the goddesses'. The simile transfers the weight of the bronze helmet to the poppy's swollen seed-head and the spring showers, setting the fertility of a garden against an early death. Leaf reports Van Leeuwen's objection that a poppy's flower and fruit stand upright despite rain, and notes that Virgil, imitating the image for the dying Euryalus ('lassove papavera collo / demisere caput pluvia cum forte gravantur', Aen. 9.436-7), avoided the difficulty by leaving out the fruit. Aesyme is otherwise unknown; Stephanus of Byzantium identified it with Oisyme on the Thracian coast (Leaf). Such brief obituaries of minor warriors, naming mother and birthplace, are a hallmark of Iliadic pathos.

title: Simile: hound and boar; Hector's Gorgon eyes
greek: ὡς δ᾽ ὅτε τίς τε κύων συὸς ἀγρίου ἠὲ λέοντος ἅπτηται κατόπισθε (hōs d' hote tis te kyōn syos agriou ēe leontos haptētai katopisthe)
short: Hector harries the fleeing Greeks like a hound snapping at the flanks of a boar or lion, killing the hindmost; his eyes are like the Gorgon's.
body: The predator image is carefully weighted: the Greeks, though fleeing, are the boar and the lion, noble and dangerous prey, and Hector is the swift hound that bites at flank and buttock and 'watches for him as he wheeleth' (Leaf on 8.340). He keeps killing 'ever the hindmost', the classic picture of a rout. The Greeks pass back through the stakes and ditch they built in Book 7 and halt by the ships, praying: the new wall is tested at once. Hector then drives his horses this way and that, 'his eyes as the eyes of the Gorgon or of Ares'. Leaf notes that for Homer the Gorgon was 'probably nothing more than a face', a petrifying gaze, as on Agamemnon's shield (11.36-7); Aristarchus read oimata, 'onrushes', for ommata, 'eyes', which Leaf thinks much less apt here.

title: Athena, Heracles and the hound of Hades
greek: ὑπ᾽ Εὐρυσθῆος ἀέθλων ... ἐξ Ἐρέβευς ἄξοντα κύνα στυγεροῦ Ἀΐδαο (hyp' Eurysthēos aethlōn ... ex Erebeus axonta kyna stygerou Aidao)
short: Athena complains that Zeus forgets how often she rescued his son Heracles during the labours imposed by Eurystheus, including fetching the hound of Hades.
body: Heracles was compelled to perform labours (aethla) for his cousin Eurystheus, king of Mycenae; Agamemnon tells how Hera tricked Zeus into this at 19.95-133. Leaf notes there is no reason to think Homer knew the canonical twelve labours, a number probably later. The labour named here is fetching 'the hound of loathed Hades' from Erebus; Homer never names Cerberus, who first appears by name, with fifty heads, in Hesiod (Theogony 311). Heracles' descent is also recalled at Od. 11.623-6 and Il. 5.395-7. Athena says she would have let him perish in 'the sheer-falling waters of Styx'; Leaf suggests the image may draw on the real Styx waterfall in Arcadia. Hades is the 'Warder' (pylartēs), keeper of the gate. Her grievance shows the gods' own memories and favours shaping divine politics.

title: Thetis' supplication and the plan of Zeus
greek: Θέτιδος δ᾽ ἐξήνυσε βουλάς, ἥ οἱ γούνατ᾽ ἔκυσσε καὶ ἔλλαβε χειρὶ γενείου (Thetidos d' exēnyse boulas, hē hoi gounat' ekysse kai ellabe cheiri geneiou)
short: Athena names the cause of Zeus' policy: Thetis' supplication in Book 1, when she clasped his knees and chin and begged him to honour Achilles.
body: Clasping the knees and touching the chin are the ritual gestures of supplication (hiketeia), performed by Thetis at 1.500-2; Athena adds that she 'kissed his knees'. Zeus' nod to Thetis set in motion the 'plan of Zeus' (Dios boulē) announced at 1.5, and Book 8 is its first full execution; Zeus himself will lay out its timetable at 8.470-7. Zenodotus and Aristarchus rejected 8.371-2 as superfluous here (Leaf). Athena's confident prediction that 'the day shall come when he shall again call me his flashing-eyed darling' (8.373) is both humorous and correct: father and daughter act together again in the final books, when Zeus allows her to help Achilles against Hector (22.183-5).

title: Athena arms: a repeated typical scene
greek: ἡ δὲ χιτῶν᾽ ἐνδῦσα Διὸς νεφεληγερέταο (hē de chitōn' endysa Dios nephelēgeretao)
short: Athena drops her embroidered robe and arms for war in her father's tunic; the whole scene repeats Book 5 almost word for word.
body: Leaf points out that 8.381-96 are taken bodily from Book 5 (5.719-21, 733-7, 745-52), a clear example of how much of Book 8 is built from lines found elsewhere. Aristarchus and Aristophanes athetized 8.385-7, and Zenodotus omitted them, because the elaborate arming leads to nothing and Zeus himself is wearing his armour (8.43); 8.390-1 were also rejected as needlessly repeated from Book 5 (Leaf). Arming, harnessing horses and the self-opening gates of heaven kept by the Hours are typical scenes, units of oral composition that a poet could expand or contract. Here the repetition also has a narrative point: in Book 5 the same two goddesses did drive into battle, so the audience expects a rerun, and Zeus stops it at the gate.

title: 'Golden-winged' Iris
greek: Ἶριν δ᾽ ὤτρυνε χρυσόπτερον ἀγγελέουσαν (Irin d' ōtryne chrysopteron angeleousan)
short: Iris, the rainbow-goddess and messenger, is 'golden-winged': the only explicitly winged deity in Homer.
body: chrysopteros, 'with wings of gold', recurs at 11.185 and in the Homeric Hymn to Demeter (314), always of Iris (LSJ). Leaf notes that this is the only mention of a winged deity in Homer and thought the conception came from the East in post-Homeric times; Hermes flies by means of magic sandals, and the other gods drive chariots. Her other epithets in this passage, 'storm-footed' (aellopos) and 'swift-footed', stress speed, and Leaf reports the scholia's remark that Iris is as quick as thought, intercepting the goddesses at the very gate of Olympus. Her name, Iris, is also the Greek word for rainbow, a fitting messenger between heaven and earth.

title: Iris repeats the message, and adds an insult
greek: ἀλλὰ σύ γ᾽ αἰνοτάτη, κύον ἀδδεές (alla sy g' ainotatē, kyon addees)
short: Iris repeats Zeus' threats almost word for word, then adds her own insult to Athena, 'fearless bitch': lines Aristarchus thought unfit for a mere messenger.
body: Homeric messengers normally deliver their message in the same words they received, changing only the persons (compare 8.402-8 with 8.416-22); the repetition is a convention of oral style that lets the audience hear the threat twice. Iris then adds: 'but most dread art thou, thou bold and shameless thing', literally 'fearless dog'. Aristarchus athetized 8.420-4 as unsuited to Iris, who always appears as a mere messenger; Leaf agrees that the case against 8.423-4 is strong, comparing the rude tone of the battle of the gods in Book 21 with Iris' courtesy when she speaks on her own account at 15.200-4. 'Dog' as an insult for a shameless woman is used by Helen of herself (6.344) and by Zeus of Hera at the end of this book (8.483).

title: Zeus foretells Patroclus' death
greek: ἤματι τῷ ὅτ᾽ ἂν οἱ μὲν ἐπὶ πρύμνῃσι μάχωνται, στείνει ἐν αἰνοτάτῳ, περὶ Πατρόκλοιο θανόντος (ēmati tōi hot' an hoi men epi prymnēisi machōntai, steinei en ainotatōi, peri Patrokloio thanontos)
short: Zeus reveals his timetable: Hector will not stop until Achilles rises by the ships, fighting over the dead Patroclus. The first mention of Patroclus' death.
body: This is the first time the poem names the death of Patroclus and the first outline of 'the plan of Zeus' in sequence: Trojan success, a battle at the ships' sterns, the death of Patroclus, Achilles' return. Zeus sets it out more fully at 15.59-77, adding Hector's own death. Murray's 'for thus it is ordained of heaven' renders thesphaton, a thing declared by divine utterance. Aristarchus athetized 8.475-6: 'on that day' should not describe the next day's events, Achilles appears at the trench rather than at the sterns, steinos means a narrow place rather than distress, and the precise dating is superfluous. Leaf thinks only the first objection has weight. Whatever the textual verdict, the prophecy turns the coming Trojan victories into tragic irony: the audience now knows that Hector's triumph is temporary and what it will cost.

title: Iapetus, Cronos and Helios Hyperion
greek: ἵν᾽ Ἰάπετός τε Κρόνος τε ἥμενοι οὔτ᾽ αὐγῇς Ὑπερίονος Ἠελίοιο τέρποντ᾽ (hin' Iapetos te Kronos te hēmenoi out' augēis Hyperionos Ēelioio terpont')
short: Zeus tells Hera he would not care if she went to the ends of earth and sea, where the deposed Titans Iapetus and Cronos sit in Tartarus without sunlight.
body: Iapetus is named only here in Homer (Leaf); in Hesiod he is the father of Prometheus and Atlas (Theogony 507-10). Cronos appears in Homer outside his role as father of Zeus and Hera only here and in three other passages (14.203-4, 14.274, 15.225), which also place him below with the Titans. Leaf warns that Homer's picture of earlier divine dynasties is vague and inconsistent; it is Hesiod who harmonises the legends. 'Helios Hyperion' uses Hyperion, 'he who goes above', as a name of the Sun himself: Homer knows nothing of the later genealogy in which Hyperion is the Sun's father (Leaf). Zeus ends by calling Hera the most shameless of all, literally 'more doglike' (kynteron), and she has no answer. Leaf offers two readings of the threat: 'go into exile, I would not miss you', or 'stir up revolt in Tartarus, I would not fear it'.

title: Night 'thrice-prayed-for'
greek: Ἀχαιοῖς ἀσπασίη τρίλλιστος ἐπήλυθε νὺξ ἐρεβεννή (Achaiois aspasiē trillistos epēlythe nyx erebennē)
short: Night falls, unwelcome to the Trojans and 'thrice-prayed-for' by the Achaeans; darkness, as in Book 7, stops the fighting.
body: trillistos, 'thrice', that is earnestly, 'prayed for' (LSJ), is unique in Homer; Leaf compares trismakares, 'thrice-blessed' (Od. 5.306). The line before has a bold metaphor: the sun falls into Ocean 'drawing black night over the earth' (helkon nykta), as if dragging a dark cloth behind it (Leaf on 8.486). Night as a power men must obey has already ended the duel of Book 7 ('it is well to yield obedience to night's behest', 7.282), and Hector echoes the phrase at 8.502 as he halts his army. The abrupt nightfall that saves the Greeks is the reason ancient critics called this book 'the cut-short battle'.

title: 'Dogs driven by the death-spirits'
greek: ἐξελάαν ἐνθένδε κύνας κηρεσσιφορήτους (exelaan enthende kynas kēressiphorētous)
short: Hector calls the Greeks dogs 'carried by the Kēres', the spirits of death, and wishes he were immortal and honoured like Athena and Apollo.
body: kēressiphorētos is unique; LSJ renders it 'urged on by the Kēres', and Leaf suggests 'hurried away from life by fate', that is, doomed. The next line, 'whom the fates bare on their black ships', spells out the compound; Zenodotus omitted it and Aristarchus athetized it as a gloss (Leaf). The Kēres are the same death-spirits Zeus weighed in his scales at noon (8.70). Leaf thought the end of Hector's speech (8.524-41) combines two versions of the same thought. Its climax, the wish to be 'immortal and ageless all my days, and honoured even as Athena and Apollo, so surely as this day bringeth evil upon the Argives' (8.538-41), repeats 13.825-8: a figure that sets an impossible wish against something felt to be certain (Leaf). In context it sounds like overconfidence on the eve of his reversal.

title: Lines from the Platonic Alcibiades II
greek: τῆς δ᾽ οὔ τι θεοὶ μάκαρες δατέοντο, οὐδ᾽ ἔθελον (tēs d' ou ti theoi makares dateonto, oud' ethelon)
short: The lines saying the gods refused the Trojans' sacrifice are not in the medieval manuscripts; they were added from a quotation in the Platonic dialogue Alcibiades II.
body: The text of 8.548 and 8.550-2 survives only as a quotation in the Alcibiades II (149d), a dialogue transmitted under Plato's name but generally thought spurious, which uses Homer to argue that the gods are not won over by sacrifices. The early editor Joshua Barnes inserted the lines into the Iliad, and Murray translates them. Leaf holds that they have 'no claim whatever to be in the text': they may come from another epic; 8.548 adapts other lines; a hasty bivouac is no occasion for solemn hecatombs; and a hatred of Troy ascribed to the gods at large contradicts the poem, in which Zeus himself loves the city (4.44-9). The verb dateonto, apparently 'tasted', also has no proper parallel. Leaf adds the irony that a spurious passage of Homer is found in a spurious dialogue of Plato.

title: Simile: the Trojan watch-fires
greek: ὡς δ᾽ ὅτ᾽ ἐν οὐρανῷ ἄστρα φαεινὴν ἀμφὶ σελήνην φαίνετ᾽ ἀριπρεπέα (hōs d' hot' en ouranōi astra phaeinēn amphi selēnēn phainet' ariprepea)
short: The Trojan fires on the plain shine like stars round the moon on a windless night, and the shepherd is glad at heart: the book's closing image.
body: For the first time the Trojans camp outside their walls, and their thousand fires, fifty men at each, appear as a serene night sky. Ancient critics objected that stars are faint around a bright moon, and one reading even turned it into a new moon; Leaf dismisses this. Lines 8.557-8, where peaks, headlands and glades stand out and 'the infinite air breaks open', repeat 16.299-300, where they suit a sudden clearing of cloud; Aristarchus and Aristophanes athetized them here and Zenodotus omitted them, but Leaf keeps them, since without them 'stars' would be awkwardly repeated. He praises the 'thoroughly Greek touch' of the shepherd's delight, which brings a human presence into the landscape. The peace of the image is ominous: the fires mark the besiegers' new confidence. Tennyson chose this passage for his 'Specimen of a Translation of the Iliad in Blank Verse' (1864).
